implementation_notes: Rails makes the column transparent: serialize :graph, coder: JSON declares that one text column holds the graph as JSON, and the framework converts on read and write, so the pattern's mapper is implicit in the attribute. It is the pragmatic default on Rails because the payload stays readable and language-neutral; binary columns and non-JSON coders remain available when the graph must be stored verbatim.
code_sketch:
class Diagram < ApplicationRecord
  serialize :graph, coder: JSON        # YAML is the historical default
end

diagram.update!(graph: { nodes: nodes })
graph = Diagram.find(1).graph          # Hash with string keys
pitfalls: Storing binary or YAML coders reintroduces unsafe loading (Psych/YAML and Marshal both deserialize classes), so keep the coder JSON unless the payload is fully trusted.
In-place mutation of the deserialized Hash/Array may not mark the record dirty, so the column is not rewritten until the attribute is reassigned.
The column type matters: a JSON coder needs a text/string column, because a bytea column cannot hold the encoded text without manual conversion.

variants.name: Marshal binary blob
variants.implementation_notes: Marshal stores an arbitrary Ruby object graph as a byte stream, so a binary column plus Marshal.dump/load is the minimal realization when only Ruby reads the payload and cycles or class instances must survive. The Ruby documentation is explicit that Marshal.load can deserialize almost any class and may therefore lead to remote code execution, and the format follows the Ruby version, so it is best kept to caches and internal state.
pitfalls: Marshal.load on stored bytes can instantiate arbitrary classes and is a known code-execution surface; never load blobs that could have been tampered with.
The marshalled format is tied to the Ruby version and to class names, so dumps may stop loading after an upgrade or a refactoring.
